lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Children's voices can change the world. Birimo's glowing map leads us to a small research harbor by the sea. There, we meet Dr. Marina Vale, a kind ocean scientist with a silver diving watch. She points to a little round submarine with thick round windows and bright lamps. This is the Bluebell, she says. I'm the pilot, so you're safe with me. Down we go! Through the porthole, the water turns from light blue to dark blue, and then to black. Dr. Vale says, Below about 1,000 meters, it is completely dark. Kiko whispers, This is the place where light never reaches. Say it with me. This is the place where light never reaches. Wonderful! Then soft blue lights appear below us. Let's read the welcome sign at the city gate. "Welcome to Deep Sea City! You are now 3,800 meters under the sea. Our city is made of glass domes, and tunnels join them together. Every dome is full of fresh air, so you can walk and breathe just like at home. Visit the gardens under our blue lamps, the Research Center, the Coral Library, and the aquarium hall with its big windows. In the Coral Library, you can find books about almost every creature in the sea. In the middle stands the Great Dome, the biggest dome of all. Please stay with your group and enjoy your visit. Our guides are always happy to help!" How deep is Deep Sea City? 3,800 meters. What is inside every dome? Fresh air. A little lanternfish with glowing blue spots swims up in a water tunnel next to us. Her voice comes from a shell speaker. Hi! I'm Lumi! She is carrying a glass lamp with six empty pearl holders. This is the Lamp of Knowledge, Lumi says. In one month, we will hold our Research Festival in the Great Dome, and young researchers will present what they found. When you learn a new research skill, a glowing pearl will appear in the lamp. Let's find out! Now, phonics. Bio means life. Biology is the study of living things. A biography is a book about someone's life. A biome is a large area with its own climate and living things. The deep sea is a biome, too! Next time, we'll visit the aquarium hall and see creatures that glow.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, This is the place where light never reaches. Today, Lumi takes us to the aquarium hall with Dr. Vale. The hall has huge windows that look out into the deep sea. Dr. Vale turns off the room lights, and we wait quietly. At first, everything is black. Then, little by little, we see tiny lights. Blue lights, green lights, and lights that blink on and off! Riko whispers, No way! Where is that light coming from? Dr. Vale smiles and says, The animals are making it. Many deep-sea animals make their own light. Scientists call this bioluminescence. Haru tries to say the long word, and everyone laughs. Then Kiko says it in a simple way. Some deep-sea fish make their own light. Say it with me. Some deep-sea fish make their own light. Excellent! Let's read the sign next to the big window. "Lights in the Dark. Down here, there is no sunlight, but you can still see tiny lights. Many deep-sea animals make their own light. Scientists call this bioluminescence. Why do they glow? Some use light to find food. Some use it to hide, and some use it to talk to each other. Others flash to scare away enemies. Look at the anglerfish in Window 3. Some anglerfish have a glowing lure on their head. The light attracts small fish, and then, gulp! Now look at Window 5. These small fish are lanternfish. Their glowing spots shine like tiny stars. There are huge numbers of lanternfish in the ocean. Please do not tap on the glass." Why do some animals glow? To find food, to hide, to talk to each other, or to scare away enemies. What does the anglerfish's lure do? It attracts small fish. Lumi swims next to the window and blinks her blue spots. Now you know my secret! I'm a lanternfish, too! Now, phonics. Bio means life. Bioluminescent means making your own light. It's bio plus luminescent, which means giving light. Lanternfish are bioluminescent. Biodiversity means the variety of living things. The deep sea has amazing biodiversity. The biosphere is all the parts of the Earth where life exists, from the highest mountains to the deepest sea. Next time, we'll find out why the deep sea is so dark.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Some deep-sea fish make their own light. Today, Dr. Vale takes us to the observation room in the Research Center. On the wall, there is a tall chart of the ocean, from the surface all the way down to the seafloor. At the top, it is bright blue. In the middle, it gets darker. At the bottom, it is black. Birimo looks out the window and asks, Why is it so dark out there? Did somebody turn off the sea? Everyone laughs. Haru guesses, Maybe the water is dirty? Dr. Vale shakes her head. Sunlight comes from above, and the water slowly takes it away. So the deeper you go, the less light there is. Then Haru says it clearly. The reason why it's dark is that sunlight can't reach this deep. Say it with me. The reason why it's dark is that sunlight can't reach this deep. Perfect! Let's read the depth chart. "How Deep Does Light Go? From the surface to about 200 meters: Bright sunlight reaches only this top part of the ocean. This is the bright part, where the water looks blue. From 200 meters to 1,000 meters: The water gets darker and darker as you go down. Below about 1,000 meters: It is completely dark. Scientists call this the midnight zone, because it is like night all the time. The water down here is very cold, about 2 to 4 degrees Celsius. The deepest known place in the ocean is in the Mariana Trench, about 11,000 meters deep. Much of the deep sea has never been explored, so there is still a lot to find out." How far does bright sunlight reach? About 200 meters. How cold is the deep water? About 2 to 4 degrees. Kiko points to the bottom of the chart. And we are here, at 3,800 meters! Lumi says, That's why my blue spots are so useful! Now, phonics. Bio means life. A biographer is a person who writes biographies, books about someone's life. An antibiotic is a medicine that kills bacteria. Anti means against. Biodegradable means it can be broken down by tiny living things called bacteria. Banana peels are biodegradable. Next time, we'll learn about the strong push of the deep water.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, The reason why it's dark is that sunlight can't reach this deep. Today, Dr. Vale shows us something we cannot see: pressure. She asks us to put our hands together and push. Push harder! Harder! That's pressure. Water is heavy, and the deeper you go, the more water there is above you. So the water pushes harder and harder. Riko looks a little worried. Is the Bluebell OK? Dr. Vale laughs kindly. Don't worry. The Bluebell and the domes of Deep Sea City are built to be very, very strong. Then Kiko asks, But what about the fish outside? They don't have strong walls! Dr. Vale opens a big research card and says, That's the amazing part. Deep-sea animals have special bodies. Say it with me. Deep-sea animals have special bodies. Great job! Let's read the research card. "Life Under Pressure. As you go deeper, the water pushes harder. Every 10 meters adds about the same push as all the air above us. At 4,000 meters, the water pushes about 400 times harder than at the surface. So how do deep-sea animals live here? First, many of them have soft, jelly-like bodies. Second, many of them have no air sacs inside. Air can be squeezed, so without air sacs, the pressure doesn't crush them. Some animals also have very big eyes to catch tiny bits of light. And look at the dumbo octopus! Its fins look like big ears. Deep-sea bodies are just right for deep-sea life." How much harder does the water push at 4,000 meters? About 400 times harder than at the surface. Why do some animals have very big eyes? To catch tiny bits of light. Birimo flaps his hands next to his head and says, Look! I'm a dumbo octopus! Lumi giggles in her water tunnel. Now, phonics. Bio means life. Symbiosis is when two living things help each other. Sym means together. Biomimicry means copying nature's ideas to make inventions. Mimic means copy. Maybe someday, people will design new submarines by copying deep-sea animals! Biofuel is fuel made from plants. Next time, it's our Deep Sea Wonder Talk, and each of you will share one amazing fact.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Deep-sea animals have special bodies. Today is our first big day in Deep Sea City: the Deep Sea Wonder Talk! We gather in the garden dome under the blue lamps. Dr. Vale, Lumi and I sit in the front row. Each friend will share one amazing fact. Lumi has one important rule. When someone shares a fact, ask, Where did you find that? Haru goes first. He holds up his hands in two big circles. One amazing fact is that giant squid have eyes as big as plates. Say it with me. One amazing fact is that giant squid have eyes as big as plates. Fantastic! Let's read our Wonder Talk cards. "Deep Sea Wonder Talk Cards. Haru: Giant squid have eyes as big as dinner plates, about 27 centimeters across. Riko: Some anglerfish have a glowing lure on their head. The light attracts small fish. Kiko: Tube worms live near hydrothermal vents, which are hot springs on the seafloor. The water there can be hotter than 350 degrees Celsius, and the worms live there without any sunlight! Birimo: Vampire squid have a scary name, but they don't drink blood. They eat marine snow, which is made of tiny bits that fall slowly from above like snow. Listeners, remember to ask each speaker, Where did you find that?" How big are a giant squid's eyes? About 27 centimeters, as big as dinner plates. What do vampire squid eat? Marine snow. Lumi asks each friend, Where did you find that? Haru says, I read it on a sign in the aquarium hall. Riko says, Dr. Vale told me. Kiko says, I saw it on a poster in the Research Center. Birimo says, I read it on a sign in the garden dome. Lumi claps her fins. Wonderful! You all know where your facts came from. Then something magical happens. The Lamp of Knowledge begins to shine, and a glowing pearl appears in the first holder! Our first pearl! Now, phonics. Let's review. Biology is the study of living things. Bioluminescent means making your own light, just like Lumi. Symbiosis is when two living things help each other. Next time, we'll visit the Research Center and choose our very own research questions.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, One amazing fact is that giant squid have eyes as big as plates. Today, Dr. Vale opens the door of the Research Center. Inside, there are glass tanks, big screens and long tables covered with maps of the seafloor. Researchers in blue coats wave hello. Dr. Vale says, In one month, you will present at the Research Festival. Every good research project starts with a question. A research question is something you really want to find out. Riko thinks about the dark water and the hungry fish. How can they find food when they can't see? She picks up a pen and writes on the whiteboard. My research question is: How do deep-sea fish find food? Say it with me. My research question is: How do deep-sea fish find food? Very good! Let's read Dr. Vale's whiteboard. "How to Choose a Research Question. Step 1: Think about what you wonder. What surprised you in the aquarium hall? What do you want to know more about? Step 2: Make it clear. Write one short question that starts with How, Why, What or Do. Step 3: Make sure you can find out. Can books, websites or scientists help you? Our team's research questions: Riko: How do deep-sea fish find food? Haru: How big can giant squid grow? Kiko: Why do some animals glow? Birimo: Do deep-sea animals sleep? Remember, a good researcher is curious, careful and honest. If nobody knows yet, that's OK. That's why we do research!" What are the three steps? Think about what you wonder, make it clear, and make sure you can find out. What is Birimo's question? Do deep-sea animals sleep? Dr. Vale laughs and says, Scientists are still finding out! Birimo's eyes go wide. Nobody knows? Then maybe I can help! Lumi does a flip and says, Let's find out! Now, phonics. Long study words have one strong part. Research. Re-SEARCH. Compare. Com-PARE. Result. Re-SULT. Summary. SUM-ma-ry. Some people say RE-search for the noun, but re-SEARCH is always fine. Clap on the strong part with me! Next time, we'll visit the Coral Library and meet a very slow, very wise friend.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, My research question is: How do deep-sea fish find food? Now we all have our research questions. But where can we find information? Dr. Vale says, Let's ask the best helper in Deep Sea City. Lumi leads us through a long glass tunnel to the Coral Library. The shelves are made of pink and orange coral, and the books glow softly under blue lamps. Behind the desk sits Mr. Oswin, a very old sea turtle with tiny reading glasses. He speaks very slowly. Wel... come... young... researchers. Haru asks, Mr. Oswin, where can I find information about giant squid? Mr. Oswin smiles and points to a poster with his flipper. Riko reads the poster and says, We can use books, websites and interviews. Say it with me. We can use books, websites and interviews. Well done! Let's read Mr. Oswin's poster. "Three Ways to Find Information. Books: Books in the Coral Library are written and checked carefully before they are printed. Use the table of contents and the index to find your topic quickly. Websites: Websites are fast, and many have pictures and videos. But anyone can make a website, so always ask who wrote it. Search online with a grown-up. Interviews: You can talk to a scientist or someone who knows a lot about your topic. Write your questions before the interview, listen carefully, and say thank you at the end. A good researcher uses more than one kind of source. And remember the most important rule in this library: Check your sources!" Why should we ask who wrote a website? Because anyone can make a website. What should we do before an interview? Write our questions. Mr. Oswin taps the last line of the poster and says his favorite words. Check... your... sources! Birimo tries to say it as slowly as Mr. Oswin, and everyone giggles. Now, phonics. Remember, long study words have one strong part. Evidence. EV-i-dence. Discover. Dis-COV-er. Explain. Ex-PLAIN. Information. In-for-MA-tion. Words that end in t, i, o, n are strong just before the ending. Information! Next time, we'll learn how to tell people where we found our information.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, We can use books, websites and interviews. Today, we are back in the Coral Library. Mr. Oswin slowly pulls a thick blue reference book from a coral shelf and gives it to Riko. It is called Lights of the Deep. Riko opens the table of contents and finds Chapter 3: Lanternfish. She reads quietly for a long time. Then she looks up with big eyes. Everyone, listen! Lanternfish swim up at night! Birimo asks, Really? How do you know? I say, That's a good thing to ask. When you share information, tell people where you found it. Then they can check it, too. Researchers often say, According to this book. Riko tries again. According to this book, lanternfish swim up at night to eat. Say it with me. According to this book, lanternfish swim up at night to eat. Excellent! Let's read the page from Riko's book. "Lights of the Deep. Chapter 3: Lanternfish. Lanternfish are small fish with glowing spots on their bodies. They are not as famous as sharks or whales, but there are huge numbers of them in the ocean. During the day, many lanternfish stay deep down in the dark water. When night comes, they swim up toward the surface to eat. Then, when the sun comes up, they swim back down again. So every night and every morning, huge crowds of little fish travel up and down the ocean. Scientists are still finding out many things about lanternfish. Maybe one day, you will help them find out more!" When do lanternfish swim up toward the surface? At night. What do they do when the sun comes up? They swim back down again. Lumi does a happy flip in her water tunnel. That's true! My cousins swim up every night! Mr. Oswin nods slowly. Good... Now you have a book and a lanternfish. Two sources! Now, phonics. Here are more study words with one strong part. Experiment. Ex-PER-i-ment. Conclusion. Con-CLU-sion. Words like information and conclusion are strong just before the ending. Observe. Ob-SERVE. Example. Ex-AM-ple. Next time, Birimo finds a very surprising website.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, According to this book, lanternfish swim up at night to eat. Today, Dr. Vale and I help everyone look for information online in the Research Center. Birimo is searching for anglerfish. Suddenly, he jumps up. Everyone, look! This website says anglerfish are as big as buses! Haru's mouth falls open. As big as buses? Riko frowns. Hmm. That sounds strange. I say, Good researchers ask questions about every website. Is it reliable（しんらい できる）? Reliable means we can trust it. To find out, we ask four questions. Who wrote it? When was it written? Does it show its sources? Can we find the same information in a book? Kiko says the first two questions out loud. Who wrote it? When was it written? Say it with me. Who wrote it? When was it written? Super! Let's read the web page Birimo found. "Fishy Fun Facts Page! Welcome to the coolest fish page in the whole world! Did you know? Anglerfish are as big as buses! Their lights are brighter than the sun! Giant squid can fly over the waves like birds! lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Who wrote it? When was it written? Now we know how to choose a research question, where to find information, how to tell people our sources, and how to check a website. Dr. Vale says, The Research Festival is in about three weeks. A good researcher makes a plan before starting. So we sit around a big round table in the Research Center and make a research plan together. Kiko writes the steps on a big card, and Riko draws a little calendar. Birimo wants to interview a giant squid, but Haru says, Maybe we should start with a scientist. Dr. Vale smiles. I'd be happy to help. Haru reads the first two steps. First, we'll read books. Then, we'll interview a scientist. Say it with me. First, we'll read books. Then, we'll interview a scientist. Wonderful! Let's read our research plan card. "Our Research Plan. Team: Haru, Riko, Kiko and Birimo. Goal: Share what we found at the Research Festival in the Great Dome. Step 1: First, we'll read books in the Coral Library. Mr. Oswin will help us find them. Step 2: Then, we'll interview a scientist. Dr. Vale said yes! We will write our questions before we meet her and say thank you at the end. Step 3: Next, we'll check one or two websites with Ms. Emma. We will ask who wrote them and when. Step 4: Finally, we'll compare our sources and write down our results. Schedule: about three weeks. Remember: Check your sources!" Who will help us find books? Mr. Oswin. What will we do in Step 4? We'll compare our sources and write down our results. We read our plan to Lumi. She swims in a happy circle and says, Let's find out! Then the Lamp of Knowledge begins to glow, and a second pearl appears next to the first one. Two pearls! Now, phonics. Let's review. Research. Re-SEARCH. It's what we're doing right now! Result. Re-SULT. A result is what we find at the end. And a biography is a book about someone's life. Bio means life, and graphy means writing. Next time, we'll learn how to say a long explanation in a short way.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, First, we'll read books. Then, we'll interview a scientist. Dr. Vale takes us to the Coral Library. Mr. Oswin, the old sea turtle, slowly pushes a thick book across the table. He looks at us over his tiny reading glasses and says, This book comes from the Research Center. Always check your sources, and this one is a good one! Riko opens it to a long page about anglerfish, because her research question is, How do deep-sea fish find food? It takes her five minutes! Then Lumi swims up to the glass of her water tunnel and says through the shell speaker, Riko, that was a lot of information. Can you say it in one sentence? Riko thinks. Then she says, In short, anglerfish use light to catch food. In short（つまり） means we keep only the most important idea and cut the extra details. Say it with me. In short, anglerfish use light to catch food. Great! Let's read the page from Mr. Oswin's book. "How Anglerfish Catch Their Food. Anglerfish live in the deep sea, where it is completely dark. Food is hard to find down there, so many anglerfish don't swim around looking for it. Instead, they wait. Some anglerfish have a glowing lure on their head, which looks a little like a fishing rod with a light at the end. The anglerfish stays very still and moves the lure slowly. Small fish see the light and swim closer, because they think it might be something to eat. Then, very quickly, the anglerfish opens its big mouth and gulps them down. Scientists are still finding out more about these amazing fish." Where do anglerfish live? In the deep sea, where it is completely dark. Why do small fish swim closer? Because they think the light might be something to eat. Haru laughs and says, In short, anglerfish are very patient! Now, phonics. When we give a talk, we pause in the right places. In short, pause, the deep sea is dark and cold. Anglerfish live in the dark, pause, so they make their own light. The animals that live down there, pause, have special bodies. As you know, pause, sunlight cannot reach the bottom. But never pause in the middle of a group like the deep sea! Next time, we'll find the big idea of a whole article.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, In short, anglerfish use light to catch food. Today, Dr. Vale invites us to the Research Center. She has written a short article for the city newspaper, and she wants young readers to check it before she shares it. Kiko reads it first. She says, There are so many facts! Which one is the most important? Dr. Vale taps her silver diving watch and smiles. Good researchers ask, What is the writer really trying to tell us? That's the main point. The other facts are details. Details support the main point, but they're not the big idea. Kiko reads the article again, more slowly this time. Then she says, The main point is that the ocean needs protecting. Say it with me. The main point is that the ocean needs protecting. Excellent! Let's read Dr. Vale's article. "The Deep Sea Needs Our Help, by Dr. Marina Vale. Much of the deep sea has never been explored. Down in the dark live amazing animals, like octopuses with fins that look like big ears and fish that make their own light. But the deep sea is not as far away from us as you might think. Scientists have found plastic even in the deepest trench, about 11,000 meters down. Things we throw away on land can end up in the ocean. If we want to keep learning about these animals, we need to take care of their home. We can use less plastic, and we can share what we learn with our families. The ocean needs protecting, and young researchers can help." What have scientists found in the deepest trench? Plastic. What can we do to help? We can use less plastic and share what we learn. Haru asks, Is the octopus with big ear fins a main point? Dr. Vale shakes her head. It's a fun fact, but it's a detail. Birimo wiggles happily and says, Well, it's my favorite detail! Everyone laughs. Now, phonics. Let's pause in the right places again. The main point is, pause, that the ocean needs our help. According to this book, pause, giant squid have huge eyes. Most of the deep sea, pause, has never been explored. Like a flashlight, pause, some fish can make light. A pause gives your listeners time to think. Next time, we'll read about something strange that falls like snow in the deep sea!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, The main point is that the ocean needs protecting. Today, we're back in the Coral Library. Outside the big window, something white is falling slowly past the dome. Birimo presses his nose to the glass. Is it snowing? Under the sea? Lumi laughs and says, Let's find out! Mr. Oswin finds a short article for us. He says, Read it, and then tell me about it in three sentences. Not more! Three sentences sounds hard, but there's a trick. Sentence one tells the topic: This article is about... Sentence two tells the most important fact: It says that... Sentence three tells why it matters: It shows... Here's Haru's summary. This article is about marine snow. It says that tiny bits of food fall like snow. It shows how deep-sea animals get food. Say it with me. This article is about marine snow. It says that tiny bits of food fall like snow. It shows how deep-sea animals get food. Wonderful! Let's read the article. "Snow in the Deep Sea. Did you know that it snows in the ocean? It isn't real snow, of course. Marine snow is made of tiny bits of dead plants, dead animals and even poop. These bits fall very slowly from the water above, like snowflakes on a quiet winter night. Down in the deep sea, there are no plants, because there is no sunlight. That means food is hard to find. So marine snow is very important. It is food for many deep-sea animals. Even the vampire squid, which has a spooky name, eats marine snow. Next time you see snow, think of the animals far below the waves, waiting for their dinner to fall!" What is marine snow made of? Tiny bits of dead plants, dead animals and even poop. What does the vampire squid eat? Marine snow. Mr. Oswin nods slowly. Three sentences, and all the important parts. Well done! Now, phonics. Here are more places to pause. In this article, pause, the writer explains marine snow. First, pause, it tells us where lanternfish live. Every night, pause, they swim up to find food. When the sun comes up, pause, they swim down again. Lumi wiggles her glowing spots. Hey, that's my family! Next time, we'll learn how to take notes without writing long sentences.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, This article is about marine snow. It says that tiny bits of food fall like snow. It shows how deep-sea animals get food. Today, Dr. Vale gives a short talk at the Research Center, and Kiko is very excited, because the talk is about her research question: Why do some animals glow? Kiko opens her notebook and starts writing every single word. Dr. Vale talks, and Kiko writes, writes, writes. Oh no! Dr. Vale is already three sentences ahead! I whisper, Kiko, you don't need to write every word. Just write the keywords. Keywords are the most important words. Kiko tries again, and now her notes look like this. Take notes: glow, food, dark. Say it with me. Take notes: glow, food, dark. Super! Short words are quick to write, and later, they help you remember the whole idea. You can draw arrows between your keywords, too, and color the most important one with a highlighter. Let's read part of Dr. Vale's talk. "Why do some animals glow? Many deep-sea animals make their own light. We call this bioluminescence. But why do they do it? Scientists have found a few reasons. Some animals glow to find food. For example, some anglerfish use a glowing lure to attract small fish. Some animals use light to hide from their enemies. Some use light to talk to each other, a bit like flashing signals in the dark. And some make a sudden bright flash to scare enemies away. Remember, it is completely dark down here, so light is a very useful tool. And there may be more reasons that we haven't discovered yet." What are the four reasons? To find food, to hide, to talk to each other, and to scare enemies away. Which word did Kiko color with her highlighter? Glow, of course! Now, phonics. Let's practice pausing one more time. If you take notes, pause, you can remember more. Write short words, pause, not long sentences. The most important word in this paragraph, pause, is glow. After you read, pause, look at your notes again. Kiko holds up her notes and says, I can remember the whole talk now! Next time, Lumi has a fun challenge for us, and we'll need a sand timer!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Take notes: glow, food, dark. Today, Lumi has a surprise for us in the aquarium hall. She swims in happy circles in her water tunnel, and her blue spots sparkle. I put a big sand timer on the table. Lumi says, It's time for the Summary Challenge! Each of you has thirty seconds to tell us what you learned. Ready? Can you summarize it in 30 seconds? Say it with me. Can you summarize it in 30 seconds? Great! Let's read Lumi's challenge card. "The Summary Challenge. Step one: Look at your notes, not at a long page. Step two: When it's your turn, turn over the sand timer. Step three: Start with your topic, and then give the main point. You can use In short or The main point is. Step four: Give one or two details, not ten. Step five: Stop when the sand runs out. Everyone listens and cheers, and nobody laughs at mistakes. Remember, a good summary is short, clear and true. If you're not sure about a fact, say so. Don't forget to say where you found your facts. Breathe and smile before you start. Good luck, young researchers!" How long does each friend have? Thirty seconds. What should a good summary be? Short, clear and true. Riko goes first. In short, anglerfish use light to catch food. Then Kiko talks about the four reasons why animals glow. Haru says, The main point is that giant squid are really big. He even gives his source. According to Mr. Oswin's book, the biggest ones measured are about 12 to 13 meters long. Birimo goes last. He says, Scientists are still finding out if deep-sea animals sleep. In short, it's a mystery! The sand runs out just as he finishes. Everybody cheers! Then the Lamp of Knowledge begins to glow, and a third pearl appears inside it. Lumi says, You learned how to summarize! Now, phonics. Let's review. In short, pause, the deep sea is dark and cold. Experiment has a strong PER: ex-PER-i-ment. Biodiversity begins with bio, which means life. It means lots of different kinds of living things. Next time, we'll start learning how to give a real presentation!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Can you summarize it in 30 seconds? Today, Lumi takes us to the Great Dome for the first time. It's huge! There are rows and rows of seats, a round stage, and a big screen. Lumi says, This is where the Research Festival will be. Young researchers from all over the city will stand right here. At the festival, each of you will give a research talk about your own research question. Haru gulps. Here? In front of all those seats? Dr. Vale laughs kindly. Don't worry, Haru. Every good talk starts with a good opening, and an opening is easy to learn. First, say hello. Next, ask a fun question to wake up your listeners. Then, tell them your topic. Riko walks to the middle of the stage and tries it. Hello, everyone. Did you know that some fish make their own light? Today, I'd like to talk about the deep sea. Say it with me. Today, I'd like to talk about the deep sea. Great! Let's read the tips Dr. Vale wrote on the board. "How to Start a Great Talk. One: Walk to the middle of the stage, stand up straight, and smile. Two: Say hello to your listeners. Good morning, everyone! is a friendly way to start. Three: Ask a question or share a surprising fact. For example, ask, Have you ever seen a fish that glows? Or share a fact, like this one: below about 1,000 meters, the sea is completely dark. This makes your listeners curious. Four: Tell them your topic. Start with, Today, I'd like to talk about... Five: Breathe! The first ten seconds are the hardest. After that, it gets easier. Your listeners want you to do well!" What should you do after you say hello? Ask a question or share a surprising fact. Why? Because it makes your listeners curious. Birimo jumps onto the stage. Good morning, fish and friends! Then Haru tries. His voice shakes a little, but he finishes, and everyone claps. Now, phonics. Ology means the study of. Biology is the study of living things, and a biologist is a person who studies them. Dr. Vale is a marine biologist! Zoology is the study of animals, and a zoologist studies animals. Say the strong part: bi-OL-o-gist, zo-OL-o-gy, zo-OL-o-gist. Next time, we'll put our points in order with first, second and finally!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Today, I'd like to talk about the deep sea. At the festival, the four friends will begin with a short team talk called Three Things About the Deep Sea, and Haru is writing it. He has a great opening now, but the rest of his talk is a mess. He has twenty facts on one long page, and they're all mixed up! Back at the Research Center, Dr. Vale hands him a small stack of note cards. She says, Write one point on each card. Then put the cards in order. Three points are usually enough for a short talk. Haru picks his three best points and lines up the cards on the table. Then he practices with three helpful words: first, second and finally. First, the deep sea is dark. Second, it is cold. Finally, the pressure is strong. Say it with me. First, the deep sea is dark. Second, it is cold. Finally, the pressure is strong. Fantastic! These words are like signs on a path. They tell your listeners where they are in your talk. Let's read Haru's note cards. "Card one. First, the deep sea is dark. Sunlight only lights up the top part of the ocean, about the first 200 meters. Below about 1,000 meters, it is completely dark. Card two. Second, it is cold. Deep water is only about 2 to 4 degrees Celsius. Brr! Card three. Finally, the pressure is strong. Every 10 meters down adds about the same push as all the air above us. At 4,000 meters, the water pushes about 400 times harder than at the surface. Many deep-sea animals have soft, jelly-like bodies, so the pressure doesn't crush them. That's also why the Bluebell has such thick walls and windows." How cold is deep water? About 2 to 4 degrees Celsius. How much harder does the water push at 4,000 meters? About 400 times harder. Kiko says, Your talk is so easy to follow now! Haru grins. And my giant squid facts can go in my own talk! Now, phonics. Ecology is the study of how living things and their homes are connected. An ecologist studies ecology. Technology means the tools and machines that people invent, like the Bluebell. Remember the strong part: e-COL-o-gy, e-COL-o-gist, tech-NOL-o-gy. Next time, we'll use pictures and a graph to make our talks even clearer!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, First, the deep sea is dark. Second, it is cold. Finally, the pressure is strong. Today, Riko is getting her talk ready in the Great Dome. Dr. Vale shows her how to use the big screen. Riko can put pictures and a graph on her slides and point to them with a long glowing pointer. Dr. Vale says, Pictures help your listeners understand quickly. But don't just show a picture. Tell your listeners what to look at. Riko clicks, and a picture of an anglerfish fills the screen. She points to the little light on its head and says, As you can see in this picture, the anglerfish has a glowing light. Say it with me. As you can see in this picture, the anglerfish has a glowing light. Excellent! Next, Riko shows a graph about depth and light. Let's read the words for her slide. "Slide Three: Light in the Ocean. This graph shows how much sunlight there is at different depths. At the top, near the surface, the water is bright and blue. But sunlight only lights up the top part of the ocean, about the first 200 meters. After that, the line goes down quickly. Below about 1,000 meters, the line reaches zero. There is no sunlight at all. This is called the midnight zone. Deep Sea City is at 3,800 meters, so it is completely dark outside the domes. In a place with no sunlight, light from animals is very important. That's why the anglerfish uses its glowing lure to find food." How deep does bright sunlight go? About 200 meters. What happens below about 1,000 meters? It is completely dark. Then Birimo, sitting in the back row, waves his arms. Riko, I can't see the bottom of the graph! Riko makes the graph bigger, and she steps to the side so she isn't standing in front of the screen. Much better! Now, phonics. Archaeology is the study of people from long ago. We learn about them from the old things they left behind. An archaeologist digs up old pots and tools. Mythology means the old stories about gods and heroes. Say the strong part: ar-chae-OL-o-gy, ar-chae-OL-o-gist, my-THOL-o-gy. Next time, we'll learn how to finish a talk with a strong ending!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, As you can see in this picture, the anglerfish has a glowing light. Today, Kiko practices her whole talk for Lumi in front of the big windows of the aquarium hall. Her opening is great, and her three points are clear. But at the very end, she just says, That's all. Bye! and runs off the stage. Lumi blinks her blue spots. Kiko, that was a bit sudden! A good talk needs a good ending, too. I explain that the ending of a talk is called the conclusion. In the conclusion, we say our main point again, so our listeners remember it. Then we can add a short message or a hope. We often start with two special words: in conclusion. Kiko thinks about her whole talk. What does she want everyone to remember? Then she says, In conclusion, the deep sea is full of surprises. Say it with me. In conclusion, the deep sea is full of surprises. Perfect! Let's read the new ending of Kiko's talk. "So why do some animals glow? Many deep-sea animals make their own light, and they use it in clever ways. Some glow to find food, some glow to hide, some use light to talk to each other, and some flash to scare enemies away. Before I started my research, I thought the deep sea was just dark and empty. Now I know that it is full of tiny lights, like stars in the night sky. Much of the deep sea has never been explored, so there may be glowing animals that nobody has seen yet. I hope you will keep asking questions about the ocean, too. In conclusion, the deep sea is full of surprises. Thank you!" What does Kiko say again in her ending? The four reasons why animals glow. What did Kiko think before her research? She thought the deep sea was just dark and empty. Lumi spins happily in her tunnel. That ending gave me goosebumps, and I'm a fish! Now, phonics. Meteorology is the study of weather. A meteorologist studies the weather and tells us if it will rain tomorrow. A volcanologist studies volcanoes, like Dr. Mori on the Island of Fire. Remember the strong part: me-te-or-OL-o-gy, me-te-or-OL-o-gist, vol-can-OL-o-gist. Next time, we'll have a big practice day in the Great Dome!

Lumi, Dr. Vale and even Mr. Oswin are sitting in the front row. Mr. Oswin came very slowly, of course, but he's here! Haru goes first with our team talk. He's nervous, so he talks very, very fast. Firstthedeepseaisdarksecondit... Nobody can follow him! Mr. Oswin raises one flipper and says, Slow down, young one. Even a turtle can win a race if he takes his time. I give Haru two tips. Speak slowly. Pause after each point. Say it with me. Speak slowly. Pause after each point. Well done! Pauses give your listeners time to think, and they give you time to breathe. Let's read the tips Dr. Vale wrote on our rehearsal card. "Rehearsal Tips for Young Researchers. Speak slowly. It may feel too slow to you, but it's just right for your audience. Pause after each point, and count one, two in your head. Look at the audience, not at your notes. Make eye contact with people on the left, in the middle and on the right. Smile! When you smile, your audience smiles too. Speak loudly enough for the people in the back row to hear you. If you make a mistake, that's OK. Just take a breath and keep going. Practice your talk three times with a friend or a family member, and you'll feel much more confident." What should you do after each point? Pause and count one, two in your head. Who should you make eye contact with? People on the left, in the middle and on the right. Haru tries again. This time, he speaks slowly, pauses after each point, looks around and smiles. Then Riko, Kiko and Birimo practice their own talks, too. When the four friends bow together, the Lamp of Knowledge glows, and a fourth pearl appears! Lumi cheers, You learned how to present! Now, phonics. Let's review. A biologist studies living things: bi-OL-o-gist. Most of the deep sea, pause, has never been explored. Discover has a strong COV: dis-COV-er. And the deep sea is a biome, a big area with its own special conditions and living things. Next time, we'll learn how to answer questions from the audience!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Speak slowly. Pause after each point. Today, we are back in the Research Center. Kiko gives her practice talk about why some animals glow. She speaks slowly and clearly, and everyone claps. Then Dr. Vale says, Now it's question time! Birimo raises his hand right away and asks, Kiko, why is it so dark down here? Kiko's cheeks turn pink. She feels a little nervous. But Lumi swims up to the window and whispers through the shell speaker, Take a breath. You know this! When someone asks you a question, you can say something kind first. That gives you a moment to think. Then you can give your answer. That's a great question. Let me explain. Say it with me. That's a great question. Let me explain. Great! Let's read the card that Dr. Vale puts on the table. "How to Answer a Question. Listen to the whole question, and don't start talking too early. Look at the person who asked it, and smile. Say something kind, like That's a great question. Then say, Let me explain. Give a short answer first, and then add one reason or one example. For example, if someone asks why the deep sea is dark, you can say that sunlight only reaches the top 200 meters or so. Below about 1,000 meters, it is completely dark. At the end, ask, Does that answer your question? Remember, a question is a gift. It shows that people were really listening to you." What should you do before you answer? Listen to the whole question. How deep does sunlight reach? About 200 meters. Kiko tries again. That's a great question. Let me explain. Sunlight only reaches about 200 meters, and Deep Sea City is at 3,800 meters. Birimo nods happily. Does that answer your question? Yes, thank you! Now, phonics. Let's read big numbers with units. 3,800 meters is three thousand eight hundred meters. 11,000 meters is eleven thousand meters. That's about how deep the deepest known place is, in the Mariana Trench. 200 meters is two hundred meters. After numbers bigger than one, we say meters with an s. Next time, Riko gets a question she can't answer. What will she do?

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, That's a great question. Let me explain. Today, it's Riko's turn. She practices her talk about how deep-sea fish find food. She talks about big eyes, glowing lights and marine snow. Then Haru raises his hand. Riko, how cold is the water outside the dome? Riko stops. She didn't write that in her notes. What can she do? She doesn't want to make up a number. Lumi says, When you don't know for sure, be honest! Tell people what you think, and tell them you're not sure. So Riko takes a breath and makes a careful guess. I'm not sure, but I think the water is about four degrees. Say it with me. I'm not sure, but I think the water is about four degrees. Great! Then Riko asks Dr. Vale to check. Dr. Vale smiles and shows us a page from her science notebook. Let's read it. "Water Temperature in the Ocean. Near the surface, the water can be warm, especially in sunny places. But the deeper you go, the colder it gets. Deep water is very cold, about 2 to 4 degrees Celsius, even in hot parts of the world. Near the North and South Poles, sea water can be as cold as minus 2 degrees. But there are surprises on the seafloor, too. In some places, there are hot springs called hydrothermal vents. The water that comes out of them can be hotter than 350 degrees! Tube worms live near these vents, and they don't need any sunlight. The ocean is full of surprises, so a good researcher always checks the facts." How cold is deep water? About 2 to 4 degrees. What lives near hydrothermal vents? Tube worms. So Riko's guess was right! Dr. Vale says, Good job, Riko. You were honest, and you made a smart guess. Then you checked it. That's what real scientists do. Now, phonics. Let's read temperatures. −2°C is minus two degrees Celsius. 4°C is four degrees. 350°C is three hundred fifty degrees. We say one degree, but two degrees, with an s. Next time, we'll learn how to ask good questions, too!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, I'm not sure, but I think the water is about four degrees. Today, Haru gives his practice talk. His research question is, How big can giant squid grow? He shows a picture of a giant squid with its long arms and tentacles. He speaks slowly and pauses after each point. Everyone listens carefully. When Haru finishes, I say, Good listeners ask good questions. A good question starts with the topic, so the speaker knows what you want to ask about. Kiko raises her hand. I have a question about the giant squid. Say it with me. I have a question about the giant squid. Great! Let's read the question guide on the wall of the Research Center. "How to Ask a Good Question. First, listen to the whole talk. Write down one or two things you want to know more about. Wait until the speaker asks for questions, and then raise your hand. Start with the topic. For example, say, I have a question about the giant squid. Then ask one clear question, not three questions at once. Good questions often start with how, why, which or where. After the answer, say thank you. If you want to know more, you can ask a follow-up question. Remember, a good question helps everyone in the room learn something new, and that includes the speaker!" When should you raise your hand? When the speaker asks for questions. What words do good questions often start with? How, why, which or where. Kiko asks, How big are its eyes? Haru answers, They're as big as dinner plates, about 27 centimeters. Then Riko asks a follow-up question. Which are bigger, males or females? Haru says, Females are bigger. The biggest ones that scientists have measured are about 12 to 13 meters long. Now, phonics. Let's read lengths. 13 meters is thirteen meters. 27 cm is twenty-seven centimeters. 11 km is eleven kilometers. That's about how deep the Mariana Trench is! Next time, Birimo gets a question, and he has a clever plan.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, I have a question about the giant squid. Today, it's Birimo's turn. His research question is, Do deep-sea animals sleep? He explains that some fish seem to rest quietly, but scientists are still finding out. After his talk, Haru raises his hand. I have a question about lanternfish. Do lanternfish sleep, too? Birimo thinks and thinks. Hmm. I don't know yet. He doesn't want to guess this time. So he says, I'll look it up and tell you later. Say it with me. I'll look it up and tell you later. Great! It's a promise, so Birimo really has to do it. After lunch, he goes to the Coral Library with me. Mr. Oswin, the old sea turtle, pushes up his tiny reading glasses. Then he opens a big encyclopedia, very, very slowly. Check your sources! he says. Let's read the page. "Lanternfish. Lanternfish are small fish with glowing spots on their bodies. There are huge numbers of them in the ocean. In the daytime, many lanternfish stay deep down, where it is dark. At night, many of them swim up toward the surface to eat, and then they go back down again. Do lanternfish sleep? Scientists are still finding out. It is not easy to watch fish in the deep sea, because it is dark and very far away. Much of the deep sea has never been explored, so there are still many questions for young researchers to answer. Maybe you will be one of them!" What do many lanternfish do at night? They swim up toward the surface to eat. Do lanternfish sleep? Scientists are still finding out. The next morning, Birimo runs to Haru. I looked it up! Haru says, Really? What did you find out? Birimo tells him everything. He kept his promise! Now, phonics. Let's read numbers with units. 400 times is four hundred times. At 4,000 meters, the water pushes about 400 times harder than at the surface. 3.8 km is three point eight kilometers. That's how deep Deep Sea City is! 100 km/h is one hundred kilometers per hour. Per means for each. Next time, Riko will be the host of a real question time!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, I'll look it up and tell you later. And Birimo kept his promise! Today, we have a practice question time in the Research Center. Haru gives his giant squid talk one more time, and Riko is the host. A host keeps question time fair and friendly. She chooses who speaks, and she watches the time. When Haru finishes, Riko stands up, smiles at the room and asks, Does anyone have any questions? Say it with me. Does anyone have any questions? Great! Riko practiced with a host card. Let's read it. "Host Card for Question Time. Thank the speaker and start the clapping. Then ask, Does anyone have any questions? Look around the whole room, smile, and speak in a clear voice. Keep question time fair and friendly. Choose one person and say, Yes, Kiko. Go ahead. Let the speaker answer. Don't answer for the speaker! If two people raise their hands at the same time, say, You first, and then you. Watch the time limit. When there are two minutes left, say, We have time for one more question. At the end, say, Thank you for all your great questions. Let's give our speaker one more big hand!" Who chooses the people who ask questions? The host. What does the host say when there are two minutes left? We have time for one more question. Kiko asks about the giant squid's big eyes, and Haru explains them clearly. Then Birimo asks a funny question. Does a giant squid ever get tired of swimming? Everyone laughs. Haru says, I'm not sure. Scientists are still finding out. I'll look it up! Everyone claps for Haru and for Riko, our wonderful host. Then Lumi's Lamp of Knowledge starts to glow. A fifth pearl appears! Only one more pearl to go. Now, phonics. Let's review. 3,800 meters is three thousand eight hundred meters. Ecology is the study of living things and the places around them. The main point is, pause, that the ocean needs our help. Biodegradable things can be broken down by tiny living things. Next time, we will read three sources that don't agree!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Does anyone have any questions? Today, Haru has a problem. He wants to say how long giant squid can grow, but he found two different numbers! So we go to the Coral Library together. Mr. Oswin puts three sources on the big stone table, very, very slowly. He says, Read them all, and then compare them. Haru reads the first two and frowns. Source A says the squid was 12 meters long, but source B says it was 13 meters long. Say it with me. Source A says the squid was 12 meters long, but source B says it was 13 meters long. Great! Let's read all three sources together. "Source A, from a book called Giants of the Sea. In this book, the writer describes a giant squid that scientists measured. It was 12 meters long. Source B, from a card in a sea museum. This giant squid was 13 meters long, from the top of its body to the end of its long tentacles. It was a female. Source C, from Dr. Vale's science magazine. How long can giant squid grow? Scientists are still finding out, because these animals live in the deep sea and are very hard to find. Most of the big ones that scientists have measured are about 10 to 13 meters long. Females are bigger than males." How long was the squid in source B? 13 meters. Which are bigger, males or females? Females. So which source is right? Maybe all of them! Each source may be about a different squid, and different squid can have different sizes. Mr. Oswin nods. Sources can disagree. That's normal. Good researchers say, Let's check more sources. Then they write down where each fact came from. Haru smiles and writes in his notes, The biggest ones measured are about 12 to 13 meters long. Now, phonics. Let's review. Biodiversity means many different kinds of living things. Compare has a strong second part, com-PARE. Every night, pause, they swim up to find food. An ecologist studies living things and the places around them. −2°C is minus two degrees Celsius. Next time, we will think about how to protect the deep sea.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Source A says the squid was 12 meters long, but source B says it was 13 meters long. Today, Dr. Vale shows us something surprising in the aquarium hall. On a big screen, there is a photo from the bottom of a very deep trench. Next to a tiny white sea animal, there is a plastic bag! Kiko gasps. How did plastic get all the way down there? Dr. Vale explains. Plastic can travel a long way in the ocean, and some of it sinks to the seafloor. Scientists have found plastic even in the deepest trench. Haru looks at the glowing fish outside the window. The deep sea is home to so many amazing animals. He says, We need to protect the places where these animals live. Say it with me. We need to protect the places where these animals live. Great! Let's read the poster the friends make together. "Protect the Deep Sea! The deep sea is dark, cold and far away, but it is not too far for plastic. Scientists have found plastic even in the deepest trench in the world. Much of the deep sea has never been explored, so we don't even know all the animals that live there yet. Here are three things kids can do. One, use less plastic. Bring your own bottle and bag. Two, share what you learned. Tell your family and friends about the amazing animals of the deep sea. Three, support careful research. When scientists study the deep sea carefully, they can find better ways to protect it. Small actions can make a big difference!" Where have scientists found plastic? Even in the deepest trench. What are the three things kids can do? Use less plastic, share what you learned, and support careful research. Lumi does a happy little spin in her tunnel. Thank you for caring about my home! Now, phonics. Let's review. The biosphere is all the parts of the Earth where life exists, and that includes the deep sea. Evidence has a strong first part, EV-i-dence. If you take notes, pause, you can remember more. Zoology is the study of animals. 200 meters is two hundred meters. Next time, we will write our own presentation scripts!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, We need to protect the places where these animals live. Today, it's time to write our presentation scripts for the Research Festival. I say, Let's practice together first. We'll write one script about Lumi's family, the lanternfish. Then each of you will write your own. Our goal is about 120 words. Our first draft is much too long. One sentence says, Lanternfish are really, really small and they are very, very cute and I like them a lot. Lumi giggles. Thank you, but that's not a fact! So we revise. First, we make it clearer. Second, we add a fact and say where we found it. Third, we cut the extra words. Here is how our talk starts and ends. Today, I'd like to talk about lanternfish. In conclusion, they are small but very important. Say it with me. Today, I'd like to talk about lanternfish. In conclusion, they are small but very important. Great! Let's read our new script. "Today, I'd like to talk about lanternfish. They are small fish that live in the deep sea. Our guide, Lumi, is one of them! First, lanternfish have glowing spots on their bodies. They make their own light. Second, they travel every day. According to a book at the Coral Library, many lanternfish swim up toward the surface at night to eat. Later, they go back down into the dark water. Finally, there are huge numbers of lanternfish in the ocean. Because there are so many of them, they are an important part of life in the sea. Scientists are still finding out more about them. In conclusion, they are small but very important. Thank you very much." Where did we find the fact about swimming up at night? In a book at the Coral Library. How long is our new script? About 120 words. Now, phonics. Let's review. A biography is a book about someone's life. Presentation has a strong beat just before the ending, pres-en-TA-tion. First, pause, it tells us where lanternfish live. An archaeologist studies things from long ago. 13 meters is thirteen meters. Next time, we will take a goodbye tour of Deep Sea City.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Today, I'd like to talk about lanternfish. In conclusion, they are small but very important. Tomorrow is the Research Festival, and soon we will say goodbye to Deep Sea City. Today, Lumi takes us on a goodbye tour, together with Dr. Vale. We wave to the glowing fish in the aquarium hall. We visit the Research Center, where we chose our research questions. At the Coral Library, Mr. Oswin waves one slow flipper. Lumi asks, What did you learn here? Riko thinks for a moment and gives a short answer. In short, we learned how to research, summarize and present. Say it with me. In short, we learned how to research, summarize and present. Great! Let's read Lumi's goodbye card. "Dear young researchers, thank you for visiting Deep Sea City! When you arrived, you asked so many questions. Why is it dark? Why do some animals glow? Then you found out the answers. You read books, checked websites and interviewed Mr. Oswin and Dr. Vale. You learned to say where you found each fact. You made short summaries and clear notes. You gave talks, and you answered questions honestly, even when you weren't sure. You also learned how to protect the deep sea. Most of all, you learned that every good answer begins with a good question. Keep asking, and let's find out together! Your friend, Lumi" Who did the friends interview? Mr. Oswin and Dr. Vale. What begins with a good question? Every good answer. At the very back of the Great Dome, Kiko suddenly stops. There is a tall old door. It is carved with dragons, castles, rabbits and stars. Kiko pushes it gently, but it is locked. Lumi says quietly, Nobody knows where it goes. Now, phonics. Let's review. Symbiosis means two living things helping each other. Summary has a strong first part, SUM-ma-ry. In short, pause, the deep sea is dark and cold. Technology means using science to make useful tools and machines. 400 times is four hundred times. Next time, it's the big Research Festival in the Great Dome!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, In short, we learned how to research, summarize and present. Today is the big day! The Great Dome is full of young researchers, scientists and sea creatures. Dr. Vale and I sit in the front row, and Mr. Oswin sits near the back in his tiny glasses. Lumi swims into the spotlight and says through the shell microphone, Welcome to the Research Festival! Let's find out! Haru talks about giant squid. Riko talks about how deep-sea fish find food. Kiko explains why some animals glow. Birimo talks about sleep, and he says honestly, Scientists are still finding out! Each speaker ends the same way. Thank you for listening. Are there any questions? Say it with me. Thank you for listening. Are there any questions? Wonderful! Let's read the festival program. "Deep Sea City Research Festival. Welcome to the Great Dome! Today, four young researchers from the land above will share what they found out. Haru asks, How big can giant squid grow? Riko asks, How do deep-sea fish find food? Kiko asks, Why do some animals glow? Birimo asks, Do deep-sea animals sleep? After each talk, there will be time for questions, so please think of a good one. Raise your hand and wait for the host. Please clap after every talk. These young researchers read books, looked at websites, asked experts and checked their sources. We are very proud of them!" Who are the four speakers? Riko, Haru, Kiko and Birimo. What should everyone do after every talk? Clap. The cheers are loud and warm. Then the sixth pearl appears, and the Lamp of Knowledge shines brightly! Behind us, the old carved door slowly opens. There is a path of glowing pages, and we can hear someone telling a story. Now, phonics. Let's review. Bioluminescent animals make their own light. Research is strong at the end, re-SEARCH. Like a flashlight, pause, some fish can make light. A volcanologist studies volcanoes. 3,800 meters is three thousand eight hundred meters. Our next adventure is in a world of stories! Goodbye, Lumi! Thank you, Deep Sea City!
